title: He bowed not (Esther 3)
hook: Mordecai won't bow to Haman, and Haman plots against all the Jews
carry: the city of Shushan was perplexed
tomorrow: For such a time as this (Esther 4:14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Esther kept her people and her kindred to herself, even after the crown. Your line was one true thing held close. What did you notice you keep close? Today, her cousin does something very different, at the king's gate. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

The king's gate in Shushan. King Ahasuerus has just raised a man named Haman above all the princes, and given an order: when Haman passes, the king's servants bow. So at the gate, they bow. Officials, servants, the whole row of them bending low as he walks by. Except one man, who stays standing. He's the same man who once walked past the women's court every day to ask after Esther. Now he stands still while everyone else bends. Today's word is what he didn't do.
screen: `THE KING'S GATE IN SHUSHAN.` → `WHEN HAMAN PASSES, EVERYONE BOWS.` → `ONE MAN STAYS STANDING.`

segments.voice: He bowed not. The verse, in the JPS 1917 translation: "And all the king's servants, that were in the king's gate, bowed down, and prostrated themselves before Haman; for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai bowed not down, nor prostrated himself before him." Day after day the servants ask him why he breaks the king's command. He gives no speech. What the text says he told them is this: that he was a Jew. That's the only reason the book offers, and it doesn't explain further. Later readers supplied reasons of their own. Some midrashic stories say Haman wore an idol, so bowing to him meant bowing to it. Others read it as Mordecai refusing to give a man the honor he owed to God alone. The text leaves the why at the edge and puts the weight on the act. Notice the turn. Yesterday Esther kept who she was hidden. Today Mordecai says it out loud, and it costs. When Haman sees that Mordecai bows not, he is full of wrath. And the story darkens. Haman thinks it beneath him to strike at Mordecai alone. He seeks to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom. Lots are cast before him, pur, to choose the day. Then he goes to the king and describes a certain people, scattered among the provinces, whose laws are different. The king hands over his ring. Letters go out. And the chapter ends with two pictures side by side: "the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city of Shushan was perplexed." The powerful drink. The city is bewildered. Haman's anger at one man who would not bend has turned on a whole people.
screen: `ALL THE KING'S SERVANTS BOWED.` · `HE TOLD THEM HE WAS A JEW.` · then, large: `HAMAN'S WRATH TURNS ON A PEOPLE.` · then: `THE CITY OF SHUSHAN WAS PERPLEXED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand upright once. If you're able, stand up now; if not, sit as tall as is comfortable. Let your feet find the floor. Lift gently through the top of your head, shoulders easy, and breathe. Notice what it feels like to take up your full height. Then think of one place in your life where you bend when you'd rather stand: a joke you laugh along with, a word you swallow. You don't have to change it today. Just stand, and feel what upright is. If you pray, you can pray standing. The bell holds the time.
Mordecai. He stays standing when everyone at the king's gate bows to Haman, and says only that he was a Jew. Today's word.
Your line: the city of Shushan was perplexed. Today, in one small moment, say plainly who you are or what you think, kindly and without a fight. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: When the scroll of Esther is read on Purim, it is a custom to drown out Haman's name with noisemakers and stamping each time it is read.

fork.setup: you're Mordecai at the king's gate. Haman is passing, and every servant around you is bowing low. what do you do?
fork.reveal: 'Mordecai bowed not down, nor prostrated himself before him.' asked why, he told them he was a Jew.

original.note: Hebrew of Esther 3:2: he would not kneel, and would not bow down.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mordecai was just being stubborn.
what it means: he would not kneel or bow to Haman, and told them he was a Jew.
what a scholar hears: the text never gives a fuller reason; some midrashic stories say Haman wore an idol.

Auditor (2026-10-01): the Judaism path quoted the KJV (3:2, 3:15); both now JPS 1917, checked against the JPS 1917 text ('bowed down, and prostrated themselves'; 'the city of Shushan').
